issue.issue_text: Whether the Bench, constituted by the Chief Justice of India in the exercise of his administrative power, has the jurisdiction to hear the matter.

facts: The petitioner challenged the jurisdiction of the sitting Bench, arguing that the Chief Justice of India (CJI) should not have constituted it in his administrative capacity.
A previous order by a Division Bench (Court No. 2) on 9.11.2017 had attempted to direct the formation of a different bench.
The petitioner's counsel argued that the CJI should neither hear the matter nor assign it on the administrative side.
law: The Chief Justice of India is the 'master of the roster' and has the sole and exclusive prerogative to constitute Benches and assign judicial business.
This principle has been definitively established by a binding decision of a 5-Judge Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court.
No other bench, whether composed of two or three judges, has the authority to allocate matters to themselves or direct the composition of a Bench.
The CJI's authority to constitute benches is a constitutional responsibility that flows from the office and cannot be dictated by the whim of a litigant.
application: The Court stated that the question of the CJI's power to form a Bench was already settled ('concluded') by the prior 5-Judge Constitution Bench decision, and this precedent was binding.
As a result, any order passed by another bench contrary to this principle, such as the Division Bench's order of 9.11.2017, was 'ineffective in law' and not binding on the CJI.

The Court rejected the petitioner's submission as an improper attempt at 'choosing a forum' and noted a contradiction in their argument, as the earlier order they relied on had included the CJI, whereas they now sought his complete exclusion.
The Court found that the CJI's action in constituting the present Bench was not only proper but a 'constitutional imperative' consistent with the law and Supreme Court rules.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the Bench had the jurisdiction to hear the matter because it was constituted by the Chief Justice of India in the correct exercise of his administrative power as the 'master of the roster,' a principle already settled by a binding Constitution Bench decision.

issue.issue_text: Whether a case can be assigned to a particular Bench by a judicial order, bypassing the administrative power of the Chief Justice of India as the 'Master of the Roster'.

facts: A judicial order was passed by a Bench of the Supreme Court directing that a particular case be listed before a specific Bench (the five senior-most judges).
This created a conflict, as the Chief Justice of India (CJI) is traditionally responsible for constituting benches and assigning cases on the administrative side.
The issue was referred to a Constitution Bench to resolve the question of whether a judicial order could override the CJI's administrative power to form benches.
law: The Supreme Court cited its own binding precedent from a Constitution Bench, which held that the Chief Justice of India is the 'Master of the Roster'.

This principle, established in cases like *State of Rajasthan v. Prakash Chand* and affirmed in the *CJAR* case, gives the CJI the sole and exclusive prerogative to constitute benches and allocate judicial business.
The Supreme Court Rules, 2013 also stipulate that the CJI is responsible for assigning cases.
This power remains with the CJI even when an allegation is made against the Chief Justice himself.
application: The Court applied the 'Master of the Roster' principle to the issue at hand.

It reasoned that since the CJI alone has the prerogative to constitute benches, no other bench, whether of two or three judges, can assign a case to themselves or direct the composition of a bench through a judicial order.
Any such judicial order that attempts to bypass the CJI's administrative authority is considered 'ineffective in law', 'not binding', and is to be ignored.
The Court concluded that the assignment of cases is an administrative function of the CJI, and it cannot be usurped through a judicial order.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the proposition that a case can be assigned to a particular Bench by a judicial order. It held that the Chief Justice of India is the 'Master of the Roster' with the exclusive administrative power to constitute benches and allocate cases, and this power cannot be bypassed or overridden by a judicial order from another bench.

issue.issue_text: Whether the conduct of the petitioners in filing the petition and seeking a specific bench amounted to unethical 'forum hunting'.

facts.fact: An organization (CJAR) filed a petition which was listed to be heard by a specific bench (presided by Hon'ble A.K. Sikri, J.).
The very next day, a member of that same organization filed a second, 'similarly worded identical petition'.
The petitioners' counsel then mentioned this second petition before a different court (Court No. 2), requesting it be heard on the same day.
The petitioners' stated reason for filing the second petition was that the first one was not being listed before their preferred court (Court No. 2).
The petitioners also alleged a conflict of interest, arguing the Chief Justice of India should not handle the case, and requested that another judge on the hearing bench recuse himself.

law.law: The Court defines 'forum hunting' as wholly unethical and unwarranted conduct.
Making allegations of a conflict of interest in order to have a matter transferred to another bench is considered a form of forum hunting.
Requesting a judge to recuse from a matter can be another attempt at forum hunting, particularly when used as a strategy to influence which judges hear the case.

application.application: The Court determined that filing a second, identical petition and mentioning it before a different court was a clear attempt to avoid the bench originally assigned to hear the matter (Hon'ble A.K. Sikri, J.'s bench).

The Court found no valid urgency to justify filing and mentioning the second petition in this manner. The proper course would have been to ask for the second petition to be listed along with the first one.

The Court viewed the allegations of conflict of interest against the Chief Justice and the request for a judge's recusal not as legitimate concerns, but as further strategies to manipulate the judicial process and steer the case away from certain judges.
The Court concluded that the collective actions of the petitioners were a deliberate exercise in trying to select a preferred bench, which is the essence of forum hunting.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted that the petitioners' conduct amounted to unethical forum hunting. It deprecated their actions, which included filing a successive, identical petition and mentioning it before a different court to avoid the assigned bench, as well as making allegations of conflict of interest and requesting a judge's recusal as a strategy to control which judges would hear their case.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Bench, constituted by the Chief Justice of India in the exercise of his administrative power, has the jurisdiction to hear the matter.
appellant_arguments: The petitioner objected to the Chief Justice of India constituting a Bench, especially one with the Chief Justice himself as the presiding Judge.
The petitioner argued that the order passed by the Bench constituted by the Chief Justice of India was required to be ignored.
respondent_arguments: The Chief Justice of India has the administrative power to constitute a Bench to hear any matter.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a case can be assigned to a particular Bench by a judicial order, bypassing the administrative power of the Chief Justice of India as the 'Master of the Roster'.
appellant_arguments: The petitioner sought an order from a specific bench (Court No. 2) to hear the matter on the same day due to urgency.
When the case was not listed before the same bench that ordered its listing, the petitioner filed a second petition to ensure it was heard by that specific bench.
respondent_arguments: Allowing litigants to choose their benches through judicial orders is an 'unscrupulous device' and a 'real threat to the very existence of the system itself'.
The assignment of cases is an administrative power of the Chief Justice of India, and bypassing it is against the settled proposition of law.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the conduct of the petitioners in filing the petition and seeking a specific bench amounted to unethical 'forum hunting'.
appellant_arguments: The petitioner's counsel argued that their actions were justified by the urgency of the matter.
The petitioner invoked the principle that 'nothing is to be done which creates a suspicion that there has been improper interference in the course of justice' to justify their conduct.
The petitioner and their counsel submitted that they were not aiming at any improper outcome.
respondent_arguments: The filing of the petition and the 'zest' with which it was pursued was an attempt to 'choose the Benches'.
The petition was 'wholly scandalous' and created a 'serious and unwanted shadow of doubt' for no good reason.
The petitioner's actions amounted to 'unscrupulous devices' and 'pressure tactics' that brought the entire judicial system to unrest.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The Chief Justice of India is the master of the roster and alone has the prerogative to constitute the Benches of the Court and allocate cases. There cannot be any command or order directing the Chief Justice of India to constitute a particular Bench.
obiter: The decisions of different benches are the decisions of the Court, and the majority opinion is the law as envisaged under Article 145(5) of the Constitution.
The Chief Justice is first among colleagues.
An institution has to function within certain parameters such as precedents, rules, and conventions for judicial discipline and decorum.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Chief Justice of India holds the exclusive administrative prerogative as the 'Master of the Roster' to constitute benches and assign judicial work. This authority is not subject to the whims of a litigant, and any attempt by a party to bypass this process by seeking a specific bench through judicial orders constitutes unethical forum hunting. Such conduct is considered a contumacious and unscrupulous device that scandalizes the court, creates doubt in the judicial system, and poses a real threat to its very existence.
legal_tests_applied: Nemo judex in causa sua: The maxim that no man is to be a judge in his own cause, which the court found was not applicable as it was 'far fetched and too tenuous to submit that any Judge of this Court... has any interest in the subject matter'.
Reasonableness of apprehension of bias: The court considered whether there was a reasonable basis for the petitioner to apprehend bias and found 'no room for reasonable suspicion even in remote'.
why_appellant_lost: The petitioner's objection to the Chief Justice of India's power to constitute a bench was rejected because this responsibility flows directly from the office, and 'none including a litigant has right to demand for contra-position'.

The petitioner's argument for recusal and the invocation of the 'nemo judex in causa sua' principle was dismissed as 'far fetched and too tenuous' and an 'argument is simply too derogatory to be made'.

The court characterized the petitioner's conduct in filing the petitions and pursuing a specific bench as 'wholly scandalous', an 'attempt at forum hunting', and the use of 'unscrupulous devices adopted by the litigants, so as to choose the Benches'.
why_respondent_won: The court affirmed that the Chief Justice of India's power to constitute benches and assign cases is a settled proposition of law, stating, 'On appointment by the President... the CHIEF JUSTICE OF INDIA becomes entitled to discharge the functions and duties of that office including constitution of benches and assignment of judicial work to judges as per procedure.'

The court agreed that allowing litigants to choose their benches is a systemic threat, stating, 'that is a real threat to very existence of the system itself and it would be denigrated in case we succumb to such pressure tactics.'
policy_considerations: The court emphasized the need for 'both the Bar and the Bench, to protect the dignity of the entire judicial system.'

The court expressed grave concern that allowing litigants to choose their benches through such tactics is a 'real threat to very existence of the system itself and it would be denigrated in case the Court succumbs to such pressure tactics.'
The court noted that the petitioner's actions created a 'serious and unwanted shadow of doubt... for no good reason whatsoever,' thereby undermining public confidence in the judiciary.
